title: Reinforcement learning for control of partial differential equations
authors: Nicolò Botteghi, Matteo Tomasetto, Andrea Manzoni
abstract: Controlling dynamical systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) remains a challenging task in scientific computing, owing to high-dimensional state spaces, distributed actuation, nonlinear dynamics, and stringent real-time constraints. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for synthesizing feedback controllers that adapt to varying operating conditions and can be deployed efficiently in real-time. This review provides a unified perspective on RL and PDE-constrained optimization, and surveys model-free, model-based, and multi-agent RL approaches to PDE control, with particular emphasis on sample efficiency, generalization across parametric variations, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. Two demonstrative examples, the stabilization of a chaotic system and a flow control problem, illustrate the performance and pitfalls of RL agents in practice. Finally, we discuss evaluation and benchmarking practices, current limitations, and open research directions toward reliable, data-efficient, and scalable RL for scientific computing.

infographic.key_insight: This review connects reinforcement learning with PDE-constrained optimization to frame adaptive feedback control of complex distributed systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: RL offers a route to efficient real-time PDE control despite high-dimensional states, distributed actuation, and nonlinear dynamics.
method: Unify RL and PDE-constrained optimization perspectives.
Survey model-free, model-based, and multi-agent approaches.
Examine sample efficiency, parameter generalization, and scalability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Chaotic-system stabilization and flow-control examples illustrate practical performance and pitfalls; the abstract reports no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Reliable deployment requires careful evaluation of data demands and robustness across operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement learning for control of partial differential equations

title: Learning developmental dynamics from lineage context
authors: Gokul Gowri, Nic Fishman, William N. Colgan, Minming Wang, Yusuke Kijima, Sachin A. Kumar
abstract: A central goal of biology is to predict the dynamics of multicellular systems. Lineage context (the states of a cell's sisters, cousins, etc.) could inform these predictions, but how best to leverage it remains unclear. Here we introduce lineage inpainting, a generative modeling approach that uses lineage context with tree-structured transformers and stochastic interpolants to model cell state dynamics across lineage trees. Applied to a lineage-traced transcriptional atlas of mouse embryogenesis, it recovers dynamics not resolved by gene expression alone, including multiple transcriptional convergence events where distinct lineages are drawn to a common state. Despite being fit on unperturbed development, lineage inpainting can generate hypotheses about perturbation responses by simulating counterfactuals. These simulations agree in many cases with observed developmental phenotypes, including a single-cell measurement of the Tbx5 knockout response. Our results show that lineage information provides a rich source of context for learning multicellular dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Lineage context helps reveal developmental dynamics, including distinct cell lineages converging on a common transcriptional state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining relational lineage structure with generative modeling offers a framework for simulating multicellular dynamics and proposing perturbation-response hypotheses.
method: Introduce lineage inpainting to model cell states using relatives' states.
Combine tree-structured transformers with stochastic interpolants.
Simulate counterfactual perturbations after fitting on unperturbed development.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a lineage-traced transcriptional atlas of mouse embryogenesis, the model recovered multiple convergence events and produced counterfactuals consistent with several observed phenotypes, including a single-cell Tbx5 knockout measurement.
infographic.watch_item: Counterfactual agreement does not establish causal validity; predictions for new perturbations require experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Learning developmental dynamics from lineage context

title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
authors: Tom Sander, Pierre Fernandez, Itai Gat, Haiming Bao, Jiaxin Shi, Jason Park
abstract: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.

infographic.key_insight: TextSeal2 strengthens distortion-free LLM watermark detection while preserving output diversity and surviving speculative decoding without changing acceptance rates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It supports watermarking in accelerated LLM serving with no measurable inference latency and no post-logits optimization.
method: Merge multiple watermark keys into one virtual key instead of selecting a key by coin flip.
Couple the virtual key to fresh noise using AutoMark’s Gaussian copula.
Verify speculative drafts with an additional exponential race on leftover draft races, using memorylessness to preserve the target distribution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three LLMs, detection improved by 8–22 percentage points over TextSeal for 100-token answers at matched diversity and a 0.001 false-positive rate; under speculative decoding, gains were 18 points over TextSeal and 22 over textGrain for 200-token answers at matched acceptance rates.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish robustness to paraphrasing or other watermark-removal attacks.
infographic.paper_title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races

title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
authors: Samuel Schmidgall, Tim Strother, Alex Bijamov, Min Woo Sun, Anil Palepu, Akshay Goel
abstract: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

infographic.key_insight: Multi-turn reinforcement learning in simulated psychiatric intake improved a language model’s interviewing, diagnostic reasoning, and safety performance compared with its identically prompted base model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Simulation offers a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing clinical conversational agents, with gains transferring to psychiatrist-enacted encounters.
method: Train with multi-turn reinforcement learning in simulated psychiatric intake environments.
Compare trained and base models in a randomized, double-blind crossover study with psychiatrist role-players and independent psychiatrist raters.
Stress-test safety using 256 adversarial presentations derived from Delphi-consensus taxonomies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of 60 matched scenario pairs (120 encounters; p < 0.0001), while adversarial testing showed acute-risk under-triage fell from 30.5% to 12.9%.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation used simulated and psychiatrist-enacted encounters rather than real-patient care; residual safety gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.
infographic.paper_title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake

title: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records
authors: Daniel Palacios, Guantong Qi, Anna Kadi, Natali Borrego, Sukru Aras, Michael L. Ferm
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are proposed for clinical prediction but are untested in pediatrics, where cohorts are small and outcomes are uncommon. Using records from 2,489 youth with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and 4,018 with type 1 diabetes (T1D), spanning structured data, note-derived social determinants and, in T1D, continuous glucose monitoring data, we predicted seven T2D outcomes, four also in T1D, at 24 months from 18 months of follow-up. CEDAR (Clinical Evidence-Driven Agent for Risk-prediction), an evidence-citing, self-auditing LLM pipeline, outperformed trained machine learning in both cohorts (pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.815 versus 0.656 to 0.700 in T2D and 0.756 versus 0.603 to 0.631 in T1D), most on the sparsely screened outcomes. Only 4 of 70,246 values it cited did not match the chart. Reading only the evidence and reasoning cited by CEDAR, two pediatric endocrinologists reached the same prediction as CEDAR in about nine of ten cases, agreeing with each other on 90.5%.

infographic.key_insight: CEDAR, an evidence-citing and self-auditing LLM pipeline, outperformed trained machine-learning models in predicting pediatric diabetes outcomes, with the largest gains on sparsely screened outcomes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evidence citation and self-auditing offer a promising design pattern for making multimodal clinical prediction systems more traceable and reviewable.
method: Combined structured records and note-derived social determinants, plus continuous glucose monitoring data for type 1 diabetes.
Used 18 months of follow-up to predict outcomes at 24 months: seven for type 2 diabetes and four for type 1 diabetes.
Compared predictive performance with trained machine-learning models and assessed cited-value accuracy and clinician agreement.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 2,489 youth with type 2 and 4,018 with type 1 diabetes, pooled AUROC was 0.815 versus 0.656–0.700 and 0.756 versus 0.603–0.631, respectively; only 4 of 70,246 cited values mismatched the chart.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish external or prospective validation; accurate citations and clinician agreement alone do not demonstrate clinical safety.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records

title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
authors: El Mustapha Mansouri, Eikichi Kimura, Masato Koga, Keigo Arai
abstract: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.

infographic.key_insight: Collaborating AI agents autonomously investigated quantum spins in diamond, checking one another’s claims and revising experiments when signal drift undermined the evidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Multi-agent review and explicit acceptance criteria offer a framework for autonomous laboratories that can detect unreliable results rather than prematurely declare success.
method: Generate and critique research questions, with authority to stop or redirect investigations.
Derive minimum calibration requirements for a defined family of microwave pulse sequences and check them computationally.
Design discriminating experiments, monitor reference measurements and revise protocols without relaxing acceptance criteria.
infographic.evidence_signal: The initial experiment matched predictions but was deemed inconclusive because of signal drift; a revised experiment met the acceptance criteria and supported the theoretical predictions.
infographic.watch_item: Demonstration on a defined quantum-spin task does not establish reliability across other experimental platforms or research problems.
infographic.paper_title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins

title: IMPACT: Inverter-Informed Multimodal Learning for Photovoltaic Generation Forecasting
authors: Anushka Katiyar, Cong Feng, Jing Wang, Tristan Liu, Simon Julien, Zachary Jacobs
abstract: This work develops a physics-informed multimodal deep learning framework for 10- to 110-minute-ahead probabilistic photovoltaic power forecasting. The forecasting model is built on a four-branch architecture that separately encodes plant-level temporal history and inverter-level spatial cloud dynamics through a graph attention encoder with a learned adjacency, known-future solar geometry, and the current meteorological state, fused through gated cross-attention. The geometry branch adds two forward-looking physical signals, spatial cloud heterogeneity and inverter ramp-down activity, each empirically weighted toward the horizon where it is most predictive. The decoder anchors its prediction to a smart persistence baseline, learning a horizon-conditioned correction, and the resulting quantile forecasts are calibrated online through a kernel-weighted adaptive conformal calibration step. The proposed model outperforms all 14 baselines, achieving a forecast skill score (FSS) of 0.2950, 0.099 above the next-best model. A branch-composition ablation shows that every branch contributes positively and the model retains substantial skill in challenging overcast and variable sky conditions (FSS 0.198 and 0.255).

infographic.key_insight: IMPACT combines inverter-level cloud dynamics with plant history, solar geometry, and weather to improve probabilistic photovoltaic power forecasts 10–110 minutes ahead.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate, calibrated short-term solar forecasts could support grid balancing, storage scheduling, and photovoltaic plant operations.
method: Encode four input branches, using learned-adjacency graph attention for inverter dynamics and gated cross-attention for fusion.
Add horizon-weighted cloud heterogeneity and inverter ramp-down signals; learn horizon-conditioned corrections to smart persistence.
Calibrate forecast quantiles online with kernel-weighted adaptive conformal calibration.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports outperforming all 14 baselines with a forecast skill score of 0.2950, a 0.099 lead over the runner-up; branch ablations show positive contributions from every branch.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify dataset scale or cross-site validation, leaving generalization to other photovoltaic plants uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: IMPACT: Inverter-Informed Multimodal Learning for Photovoltaic Generation Forecasting

title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization
authors: Mads Toftrup, Marco Federici, Boris van Breugel, Paul Whatmough, Markus Nagel
abstract: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.

infographic.key_insight: A unified Hessian-guided objective jointly optimizes quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding to account for their effects on model outputs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets more accurate low-bit LLM deployment while reducing memory footprint and computational cost.
method: Approximate output changes from joint weight and activation quantization using Hessian information.
Use a tractable Fisher approximation to capture output sensitivity.
Jointly optimize ranges, transformations, and rounding under a shared objective.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent gains over state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods in channel-wise and block-wise settings, but provides no numerical results or benchmark details.
infographic.watch_item: The accuracy–cost trade-off of the Fisher approximation needs verification for the intended model and deployment setting.
infographic.paper_title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization

title: Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns
authors: Eric Rudolph, Philipp Steigerwald, Jens Albrecht
abstract: This study investigates the capabilities of Large Language Models to simulate counselling clients in educational role-plays in comparison to human role-players. Initially, we recorded role-playing sessions, where novice counsellors interacted with human peers acting as clients, followed by role-plays between humans and clients simulated by Mistrals Mixtral 8x7b using 4-bit quantization. These interactions were analysed with a counselling communication pattern system at sentence level. We investigated two key questions: (1) to what extent LLM-generated responses replicate authentic conversational dynamics and (2) whether counsellors' communication behaviour differs when interacting with human versus LLM-simulated clients. The findings highlight both similarities and differences in the application of counselling patterns across scenarios, showing the potential of LLM-based role-playing exercises to enhance counselling competencies and to identify areas for further refinement in virtual client simulations.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-simulated clients show both similarities and differences to human role-players in counselling communication patterns, suggesting potential for training without establishing equivalence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Virtual counselling clients could support training systems, but their conversational patterns should be evaluated against human role-play before deployment.
method: Record novice counsellors interacting with human peers acting as clients.
Conduct human–LLM role-plays using Mixtral 8x7B with 4-bit quantization.
Analyse sentence-level counselling patterns and compare interactions across client types.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports similarities and differences across human-client and LLM-client sessions but provides no sample sizes, effect sizes, or quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish whether observed conversational similarities translate into improved counselling competencies.
infographic.paper_title: Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns

title: Uncertainty-aware Feedback Loop Diagnosis: integrating reinforcement learning and conformal prediction for reliable wafer defect classification
authors: Aleksandr Dekhovich, Carlas Smith, Oleg Soloviev
abstract: Semiconductor manufacturing is a complex, multi-step process that requires both high precision and low operating costs. Therefore, detecting defects in a high-volume setting is an important component of wafer map analysis for reliable production. However, most state-of-the-art deep learning approaches require a full scan of the surface, which hinders the development of high-throughput inspection systems. To address this problem, we propose Uncertainty-aware Feedback Loop Diagnosis (UFLD), a novel algorithm that employs reinforcement learning for adaptive measurement acquisition and provides a prediction uncertainty level after each step, stopping the process once sufficient information is obtained. Unlike existing methods that rely on ensemble models or auxiliary confidence estimation deep learning models, UFLD utilizes a more parameter-efficient conformal prediction framework to determine the optimal stopping time. The proposed UFLD reduces acquisition time by about $40\%$ and achieves $98.4\%$ inspection accuracy, without requiring an additional learned confidence-estimation network. We validated our approach on the MixedWM38 dataset, demonstrating its advantages over existing adaptive acquisition procedures and standard convolutional neural networks.

infographic.key_insight: UFLD combines reinforcement learning with conformal prediction to classify wafer defects from adaptive measurements and stop when sufficient information is obtained.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive inspection could improve semiconductor production throughput by reducing acquisition time without requiring an additional learned confidence-estimation network.
method: Use reinforcement learning to select measurements adaptively.
Apply conformal prediction to quantify uncertainty after each acquisition step.
Stop acquisition once sufficient information supports classification.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MixedWM38, the authors report about 40% lower acquisition time and 98.4% inspection accuracy, with comparisons against existing adaptive acquisition procedures and standard CNNs.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment should validate uncertainty calibration and stopping behavior under shifts in defect patterns and measurement conditions beyond MixedWM38.
infographic.paper_title: Uncertainty-aware Feedback Loop Diagnosis: integrating reinforcement learning and conformal prediction for reliable wafer defect classification

title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment
authors: Art Kanke
abstract: Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, proposes minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents' first choices match the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run remains limited. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste.

infographic.key_insight: Research agents propose worthwhile experiments, but evidence that their rankings improve which experiments to run remains limited.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Use research agents to generate experiment candidates, but validate their prioritization before committing compute or adopting costlier agent teams.
method: Six frontier models, working alone or in teams, proposed minimum viable experiments for seven recent NLP papers.
Agents set pass thresholds, forecast outcomes and rank experiments before execution.
A separate executor attempted every experiment, including last-ranked ones, and three model auditors judged results.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of 415 experiments, auditors judged 194 sound, valuable and new, with 73 also beyond the seed paper and non-obvious; agents’ top choices beat random selection but showed no demonstrated advantage over choosing the first-written experiment.
infographic.watch_item: Outcomes were judged by model auditors, and teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality.
infographic.paper_title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment

title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
authors: Alan Sorani, Ashvni Narayanan, Michael Shalyt, Tali Monderer, Rotem Kalisch, Hila Barkan
abstract: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.

infographic.key_insight: An AI-assisted pipeline improves evaluation of research-level mathematical proofs across natural language, CAS code, and Lean formalizations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a methodology for evaluating complex mathematical reasoning and supporting code at scale in AI-for-science workflows.
method: Analyze Ramanujan Challenge submissions on research-level number theory problems.
Evaluate semantic and logical correctness across natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations.
Compare pipeline judgments with conventional one-shot LLM judgments.
infographic.evidence_signal: The pipeline reduced false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and increased supporting-code judgment accuracy from 46% to 58%.
infographic.watch_item: Supporting-code judgment accuracy remains only 58%, and generalization beyond this number theory benchmark is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs

title: Aerodynamic Shape Optimization of unsteady flapping wings
authors: Hamid R. Karbasian, Brian C. Vermeire
abstract: This study introduces a new approach for building surrogate models, in the form of Reduced Order Models (ROMs), for PDE-constrained optimization. A physics-constrained data-driven framework is developed to transform large-scale non-linear optimization problems into ROM-constrained optimization problems. Unlike conventional methods, which suffer from instability of the forward sensitivity function, the proposed approach projects optimization problems to system dynamics optimization problems in Hilbert space to increase stability, diminish memory requirements, and lower computational cost. The present approach is applied to shape optimization of a 2D flapping wing section at $Re=2,400$, where the non-linear interaction of the wing with fluid includes chaotic flow structures. It is shown that the proposed approach can significantly enhance the time-averaged thrust force and propulsive efficiency by 37\% and 40\%, respectively. We also tested this approach for a 3D flapping wing and the results reveal the potential of the proposed approach for more complex optimal designs in the aerospace industry.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-constrained, data-driven reduced-order modeling framework enables flapping-wing shape optimization, improving time-averaged thrust by 37% and propulsive efficiency by 40%.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce computational and memory costs for aerodynamic design optimization involving unsteady, nonlinear flows.
method: Build physics-constrained, data-driven reduced-order models of flow dynamics.
Project PDE-constrained optimization into system dynamics optimization in Hilbert space.
Optimize wing shapes using reduced-order constraints to mitigate forward-sensitivity instability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 37% higher time-averaged thrust and 40% higher propulsive efficiency for a 2D flapping wing at Re = 2,400, plus a 3D demonstration.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify 3D performance gains or establish reliability beyond the tested flow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Aerodynamic Shape Optimization of unsteady flapping wings

title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
authors: Qiushi Sun, Da Yu, Alexander Knop, Amer Sinha, Lingpeng Kong, Ben Kao
abstract: Building and scaling computer-using agents (CUAs) across desktop, mobile, and web environments requires reliable task-completion verification for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Typical automated approaches prompt vision-language models (VLMs) to judge trajectories or generate programs to inspect application state. However, both rely on partial views of complex digital environments. VLM judges are restricted to supplied observations, while generated programs depend on accessible state. These views can omit decisive evidence or leave completion judgments unsupported. Tailoring separate verifiers to different platforms and access settings adds further engineering cost. We present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework for verification through agentic exploration. It treats verification as dynamic evidence gathering and assessment within a shared procedure for online and offline settings across platforms and observation modalities. After inspecting the available context to construct a task rubric, the verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines their findings under explicit evidence rules. Experiments show improved agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines across these settings, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online. Further analyses connect these gains to complementary evidence and test-time exploration.

infographic.key_insight: VeriCUA verifies computer-agent task completion by actively gathering evidence rather than judging only fixed observations or accessible application state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A shared verification procedure across desktop, mobile, and web environments could reduce platform-specific engineering for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning.
method: Inspect available context and construct a task-completion rubric.
Select GUI or code checks to investigate unresolved requirements.
Combine findings under explicit evidence rules in online and offline settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments report better agreement with reference labels than compared baselines, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online.
infographic.watch_item: Active exploration introduces additional checks whose runtime cost and dependence on available GUI or code access should be assessed in deployment.
infographic.paper_title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents

title: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Mobile Money Scan Messages in Ghana: A Comparative Evaluation of Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and Randon Forest Classifiers
authors: Ibrahim Salifu, Muhaisin Tiyumba Nantogmah
abstract: Mobile money (MoMo) is Ghana's preferred retail payment channel, recording GHC518.4 billion in transactions in December 2025 and over 26.7 million active accounts (Graphic Online, 2026). This growth has coincided with increased social-engineering fraud over Short Message Service (SMS) and Unstructured Supplementary Service Data (USSD), where fraudsters impersonate network operators, agents, relatives, or regulators to obtain personal identification numbers (PINs), identity data, or funds. We present a supervised machine-learning pipeline for classifying scam and legitimate Ghanaian MoMo SMS messages using a labelled corpus of 220 messages across 18 scam and legitimate subcategories. Domain-specific normalisation of currency amounts, phone numbers, and USSD codes preceded TF-IDF vectorisation of unigrams and bigrams. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation and a 20% held-out test set, we trained and evaluated Multinomial Naive Bayes, linear support vector machine (SVM), and Random Forest classifiers using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). Held-out accuracy, F1, and AUC were 1.00 for Naive Bayes and linear SVM; cross-validated accuracy averaged 96.6% (+/-3.3), 94.9% (+/-4.6), and 92.0% (+/-4.2). Discriminative n-grams reflected imperative urgency ("send," "claim," "please send") and PIN solicitation ("PIN," "pincode"); legitimate messages featured confirmatory and cautionary language ("balance," "successful," "do not share"). Findings are contextualised in Sub-Saharan African SMS fraud detection, small template-based corpus ceiling effects, and a pathway toward larger naturalistic multilingual corpora. Interpretable classical classifiers achieve high accuracy on structured MoMo scam text and suit carrier- or handset-level filtering in low-resource, on-device settings.

infographic.key_insight: Naive Bayes and linear SVM achieved perfect held-out accuracy on a small Ghanaian mobile-money SMS corpus, showing promise for scam detection.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Classical text classifiers offer a lightweight approach to carrier- or handset-level scam filtering in resource-constrained settings.
method: Normalise currency amounts, phone numbers, and USSD codes.
Encode SMS text with TF-IDF unigrams and bigrams.
Compare Multinomial Naive Bayes, linear SVM, and Random Forest.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 220 labelled messages in 18 subcategories, stratified five-fold cross-validation yielded mean accuracies of 96.6% for Naive Bayes, 94.9% for SVM, and 92.0% for Random Forest; Naive Bayes and SVM reached 1.00 accuracy, F1, and AUC on a 20% held-out test set.
infographic.watch_item: The small, template-based corpus may inflate performance; validate on larger, naturalistic multilingual messages before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Mobile Money Scan Messages in Ghana: A Comparative Evaluation of Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and Randon Forest Classifiers

title: On the Fundamental Limits of Prefill-Based Decoding Length Prediction
authors: Haowen Shi, Xuzhe Yan, Fahao Chen, Peng Li
abstract: Predicting how many tokens a large language model (LLM) will decode, using only prefill-phase hidden states, is a key primitive for inference scheduling. We show that current benchmarks conflate predictor quality with task hardness: when the target model, dataset, or sampling configuration changes, reported accuracy collapses even though the predictor is unchanged. We trace this instability to an overlooked error source---the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding---and derive bounds that every prefill-side method must obey. Our analysis treats decoding as a stopped stochastic process. The per-step stopping probability of a response is not constant but ramps up over hundreds of steps, so the decode length inherits a central limit theorem from the many local decisions that determine where a response ends; this yields per-prompt normality with an explicit error term, together with an affine variance law $σ=αμ+b$ whose slope is the coefficient of variation of the number of response segments. Empirically, the normal law reproduces the per-prompt MAE and the central mass of the decode-length distribution to within a few percent, and the residual departures from normality (mild right skew, slight excess kurtosis) are the ones predicted by the sampling-noise correction. Under fixed model, data, and sampling conditions, a broad design space of predictors (MLP, EGTP, FiLM, soft-label, and Mixture-of-Experts variants) converges to similar performance close to the bound, confirming that \emph{system error dominates model error}. We argue for a benchmarking protocol that fixes the model, data, and sampling parameters and that reports relative-error metrics alongside absolute ones. Code and analysis tools are available at https://github.com/ShwStone/DecodingPredict.

infographic.key_insight: Inherent randomness in autoregressive decoding imposes a fundamental error floor on length prediction from prefill hidden states, with system error dominating predictor error in the evaluated settings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Inference schedulers should account for irreducible length uncertainty rather than expect more complex prefill predictors to eliminate prediction error.
method: Model decoding as a stopped stochastic process with a time-varying stopping probability.
Derive per-prompt approximate normality, an explicit approximation error, and the affine standard-deviation law σ = αμ + b.
Compare diverse predictor architectures against theoretical error bounds under fixed model, data, and sampling conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The normal approximation reproduces per-prompt MAE and central distribution mass within a few percent, while evaluated predictor variants achieve similar performance close to the bound.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on model, dataset, and sampling configuration; fix these conditions and report relative as well as absolute errors for meaningful comparisons.
infographic.paper_title: On the Fundamental Limits of Prefill-Based Decoding Length Prediction

title: The Precision Wall: An Optimizer-Dependent Boundary for Optimization under Power-Law Measurement Spectra
authors: Lngel Kyo
abstract: In low-rank matrix sensing of a rank-$D$ factor $U^\ast \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times D}$, replacing isotropic Gaussian designs with power-law measurement covariance $Σ= \mathrm{diag}(j^{-s})_{j=1}^V$ leaves the Burer--Monteiro landscape free of spurious local minima, yet division-normalised first-order optimizers stall above a critical exponent $s^\ast$. We trace this failure to a numerical precision wall. At the ground truth, the smallest non-gauge expected Hessian eigenvalue scales at leading order as $V^{-(s+1)}D^{-s}$. When this curvature drops below the effective denominator floor $ε_O$ of optimizer $O$, normalisation noise overwhelms rare-direction gradients, yielding the leading-order boundary $s^\ast_O(V, D) = [\log(1/ε_O) - \log V]/\log(VD) + δ_O$, where $δ_O$ is a metric-dependent detection lag. With $δ_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ calibrated on four configurations and frozen, this formula predicts Adam's onset within $0.45$ across all 16 cells of a held-out grid ($V \in \{64,128,256,512\} \times D \in \{4,8,16,32\}$), separates fixed-$VD$ pairs, and distinguishes denominator-precision walls from conditioning and sign-quantisation walls. The approximation fails at $D = 2$, reflects a finite-$D$ spectral crossover, and saturates below $\varepsilon_0 = 10^{-8}$ at a dynamical floor.

infographic.key_insight: Power-law measurement spectra preserve a spurious-minimum-free landscape but can push curvature below an optimizer’s effective denominator floor, creating an optimizer-dependent precision wall.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizer denominator precision can limit recoverability even when the optimization landscape has no spurious local minima.
method: Study rank-D Burer–Monteiro matrix sensing with measurement covariance Σ = diag(j^−s).
Derive leading-order minimum non-gauge curvature scaling as V^−(s+1)D^−s.
Predict the critical exponent from the optimizer’s effective denominator floor and a calibrated detection lag.
infographic.evidence_signal: After calibrating Adam’s detection lag on four configurations, the formula predicted onset within 0.45 in exponent s across all 16 held-out V × D configurations and distinguished fixed-VD pairs.
infographic.watch_item: The approximation fails at D = 2, and reducing the denominator floor below 10^−8 encounters a dynamical saturation floor.
infographic.paper_title: The Precision Wall: An Optimizer-Dependent Boundary for Optimization under Power-Law Measurement Spectra

title: Framework-Conditional Open Materials Generation
authors: Maya M. Martirossyan, Hillary Pan, Philipp Höllmer, Stefano Martiniani
abstract: Theoretical predictions of novel materials rely on a variety of techniques, from data-mining-based ion substitution methods to fully de novo generative models. Each approach imposes specific constraints and encounters unique challenges when extrapolating beyond the distribution of known materials to discover new ones. The foremost goal of materials generation is to produce stable, unique, and novel (S.U.N.) structures. Predicted structures that meet these criteria, however, typically result from novel chemical compositions mapped onto known structural prototypes or frameworks. We leverage this heuristic insight to present a new generative paradigm for the de novo prediction of inorganic crystalline materials constrained by their structural framework---i.e., the unit cell shapes and respective particle positions. Our method, termed OMatG-FC (Open Materials Framework-Conditional Generation), learns via a combination of discrete flow matching on the atomic species and stochastic interpolants for the volume scaling of the unit cell lattice, while fixing in-place the fractional coordinates and the unit-volume lattice vectors, dramatically reducing the dimensionality of the problem compared to unconstrained (framework-free) generation. Our method is more flexible than existing prototype-constrained methods, demonstrating capability for discovery of unseen, stable prototypes derived from known structural frameworks. We also investigate the number of unique frameworks in the MP-20 dataset, demonstrating the propensity of duplicate frameworks within the dataset and providing a framework-split version. We benchmark the performance of our model using the LeMat-GenBench suite using three ML interatomic potentials and achieve state-of-the-art S.U.N. rate below the convex hull, eschewing the need to learn atomic packings for materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: OMatG-FC generates inorganic crystals by learning atomic species and cell volume on fixed structural frameworks, achieving a reported state-of-the-art stable, unique, and novel (S.U.N.) rate below the convex hull.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fixing atomic packing reduces the generation problem’s dimensionality while retaining flexibility to discover unseen stable prototypes from known frameworks.
method: Condition generation on fixed fractional coordinates and unit-volume lattice vectors.
Use discrete flow matching for atomic species and stochastic interpolants for cell-volume scaling.
Identify duplicate frameworks in MP-20 and provide a framework-split dataset.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation uses LeMat-GenBench with three ML interatomic potentials; the abstract reports state-of-the-art S.U.N. performance but gives no numerical rates.
infographic.watch_item: Fixed-framework conditioning limits exploration of new atomic packings, and predicted stability still requires validation beyond ML interatomic potentials.
infographic.paper_title: Framework-Conditional Open Materials Generation

title: Composing and Steering Diffusion Models with Generalized Feynman-Kac Correctors
authors: Wael Mattar, Daniel Freedman
abstract: Diffusion models have become the leading paradigm in generative modeling, yet many applications require sampling from distributions that are not those of any single pretrained model, but are instead defined through combinations of several models, possibly tilted toward high values of a downstream reward. Naively combining the scores of the models yields incorrect samples, while existing corrections are restricted to specific families of targets. In this work, we introduce the generalized Feynman-Kac correctors (GFKC), a principled framework for sampling from an arbitrary target function of several pretrained diffusion models. We show that the geometric interpolation between an arbitrary initial function and the target function of the models satisfies a Feynman--Kac partial differential equation, and derive its potential in closed form. To evaluate this potential during generation, we further generalize the log-probability ODE to track the density of each model along trajectories driven by a different velocity field. The resulting algorithm operates entirely in the log domain, incorporates reward-based steering at no additional conceptual cost, and corrects the generation on the fly, without retraining or fine-tuning the models. We validate the method on analytic Gaussian models, where it closely matches the ground-truth targets, and on diffusion models trained on MNIST, where it samples from non-trivial combinations of the models and enables effective steering.

infographic.key_insight: Generalized Feynman-Kac correctors enable principled sampling from arbitrary functions of multiple pretrained diffusion models, including reward-steered targets, without retraining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework lets practitioners compose and steer existing diffusion models while correcting sampling errors introduced by naive score combination.
method: Derive a Feynman-Kac PDE and closed-form potential for geometric interpolation from an initial function to the target.
Generalize the log-probability ODE to track each model’s density along trajectories driven by a different velocity field.
Apply corrections during generation entirely in the log domain, with optional reward-based steering.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on analytic Gaussian models closely match ground-truth targets, while MNIST experiments demonstrate non-trivial model combinations and effective steering.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence in the abstract is limited to Gaussian and MNIST settings; scalability and computational overhead for larger models remain unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Composing and Steering Diffusion Models with Generalized Feynman-Kac Correctors

title: The Athlete as a Scientist of One: Agentic Bayesian Experimental Design for Individualized Physiology from Consumer Wearables
authors: Behnam Moradi
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for personal health read wearable data and recommend, but do not learn about the individual in a way that can be audited or falsified. We present EpiCoach, an agentic system that treats one athlete, a cross-country mountain biker, as the subject of accountable N-of-1 science. Claims about the athlete live in an evidence-gated hypothesis registry: each must issue a probabilistic prediction about a future session before it occurs, and its belief moves only through computed evidence from a logged statistical fit. Predictions come from a mechanistic digital twin inferred from heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude: a lagged heart-rate response model, a fitness-fatigue model with learned time constants, and a latent technical-descending skill state, measured on discovered trail segments. The agent prescribes the next training week as a constrained experiment maximizing information gain subject to load and safety constraints, around two instrument rides. We evaluate the system two ways over eighteen months of data. A rolling-origin replay benchmark shows the twin beats standard forecasters on heart rate but not segment time, and the agentic loop matches a static model. A live prospective phase runs the weekly cycle: in its first three weeks the ledger sealed 20 predictions, scored 14, the descent forecast calibrated after one correction, the climb forecast pessimistic as the athlete improved, and the safety officer vetoed the agent twice. Every correction is preserved in the registry, a template for auditable, falsifiable personalization in digital health. We release the registry, benchmark and protocol.

infographic.key_insight: EpiCoach turns wearable-based coaching into auditable N-of-1 science by requiring predictions before sessions and updating beliefs only from logged statistical evidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The system offers a design pattern for personalized health agents that connect mechanistic models, falsifiable predictions, constrained experiments and safety oversight.
method: Infer a digital twin from heart rate, GPS and altitude, modeling cardiac lag, fitness–fatigue dynamics and technical-descending skill.
Maintain an evidence-gated hypothesis registry with prospective probabilistic predictions and traceable belief updates.
Plan weekly training to maximize information gain within load and safety constraints, centered on two instrument rides.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation used 18 months of one athlete’s data: replay beat standard forecasters on heart rate but not segment time, while the first three live weeks sealed 20 predictions, scored 14 and recorded two safety vetoes.
infographic.watch_item: Generalizability remains untested beyond one athlete, and the agentic loop matched rather than outperformed a static model in replay.
infographic.paper_title: The Athlete as a Scientist of One: Agentic Bayesian Experimental Design for Individualized Physiology from Consumer Wearables
